title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Two enemy shells had already flown across the bridge, where a crush of men was building up. Halfway across, Prince Nesvitski had dismounted and now found his bulky body jammed against the railings. He glanced back, laughing, at the Cossack standing a few steps behind him holding two horses by their bridles. Every time Nesvitski tried to push forward, soldiers and carts shoved him back against the railings, and all he could do was smile.

"Some friend you are!" the Cossack said to a supply wagon driver who was pressing into the infantrymen crowded around his wheels and horses. "What kind of fellow are you? Can't you wait a moment? Don't you see the general needs to get through?"

But the wagon driver paid no attention to the word "general" and shouted at the soldiers blocking his way. "Hey, boys! Keep to the left! Hold up!" But the soldiers, packed shoulder to shoulder with bayonets interlocking, moved across the bridge in a solid mass. Looking over the railing, Prince Nesvitski watched the quick, noisy little waves of the Enns rippling and swirling around the bridge pilings, chasing one another downstream. Looking at the bridge itself, he saw an equally unbroken living wave of soldiers—shoulder straps, covered shakos, knapsacks, bayonets, long muskets, and beneath the shakos, faces with broad cheekbones, hollow cheeks, and dull, tired expressions—and feet trudging through the sticky mud that coated the bridge planks. Sometimes, through this monotonous stream of men, like a fleck of white foam on the river's current, an officer in a cloak, with a face of a different type, squeezed his way through. Sometimes, like a wood chip spinning in the water, a dismounted hussar, an orderly, or a civilian was carried along in the flood of infantry. And sometimes, like a log drifting downstream, an officers' or company baggage wagon—piled high, covered in leather, and hemmed in on every side—rolled across the bridge.
"It's like a dam burst," said the Cossack, giving up hope. "Are there many more of you coming?"
"A million, all but one!" a wisecracking soldier in a torn coat called back with a wink, and passed on, followed by another—an old man.
"If he"—meaning the enemy—"starts firing at the bridge now," the old soldier said glumly to a comrade, "you'll forget all about scratching yourself."
That soldier moved on, and after him came another riding on a cart.
"Where the hell have the leg wrappings been shoved?" an orderly shouted, running behind the cart and rummaging in the back of it.
He too passed on with the wagon. Then came a group of soldiers who had clearly been drinking.
"And then, old fellow, he smacks him right in the teeth with the butt of his rifle..." a soldier with his greatcoat tucked up tight was saying cheerfully, swinging his arm wide.
"Yeah, and that ham was delicious..." another replied with a loud laugh. And they too moved on, so that Nesvitski never learned who had been hit in the teeth, or what ham had to do with any of it.
"Bah! Look at them scurry. One cannonball and they think they're all going to die," a sergeant was saying angrily and reproachfully.

"When it flies past me, Papa—the ball, I mean," said a young soldier with an enormous mouth, barely holding back his laughter. "I felt like I was going to die of fright. I really did, honest to God, I was that scared!" he said, as if boasting about having been frightened.

He too passed on. Then came a cart unlike any of the others. It was a German cart pulled by a pair of horses and led by a German, loaded with what looked like an entire household's belongings. A fine brindled cow with a large udder was tied to the back. A woman carrying an infant, an old woman, and a healthy German girl with bright red cheeks sat perched on feather beds. These refugees had evidently been allowed through by special permission. Every soldier's eyes turned toward the women, and as the cart crawled past at walking pace, every remark the soldiers made was about the two younger ones. Each face wore almost the same grin, reflecting thoughts that were anything but proper.
"Look at that—even the German sausage is clearing out!"
"How about selling me the missus?" another soldier called to the German, who strode along angrily and nervously with his eyes fixed on the ground.
"Look how she's dressed herself up! The devils!"
"Hey, Fedotov—they should quarter you with them!"
"I've seen plenty of that before, mate!"
"Where are you headed?" asked an infantry officer who was eating an apple, also half smiling as he looked at the pretty girl.
The German closed his eyes, indicating he didn't understand.
"Here, take this if you'd like," said the officer, holding out the apple to the girl.

The girl smiled and took it. Nesvitski, like every other man on the bridge, kept his eyes on the women until they had passed. When they were gone, the same stream of soldiers continued with the same kind of chatter, and finally everyone came to a halt. As so often happens, the horses pulling a supply wagon had balked at the end of the bridge, and the entire crowd was forced to wait.

"Why have they stopped? No order at all!" the soldiers grumbled. "Where do you think you're shoving? To hell with you! Can't you wait? It'll be even worse if he sets fire to the bridge. Look—there's an officer stuck too." Different voices in the crowd said these things as the men looked at one another and all pressed toward the far end of the bridge.
Looking down at the waters of the Enns beneath the bridge, Nesvitski suddenly heard a new sound—something approaching fast, something large that splashed into the water.
"See where that one landed!" a soldier nearby said grimly, glancing around at the sound.
"Encouraging us to move faster," said another nervously.
The crowd surged forward again. Nesvitski realized it had been a cannonball.
"Hey, Cossack! My horse!" he called. "Now then, make way! Get out of the way!"

With enormous difficulty he reached his horse, and shouting nonstop, he pushed forward. The soldiers squeezed aside to let him through but immediately pressed in on him again, jamming his leg. Those nearest him weren't to blame—they were being crushed from behind even harder.
"Nesvitski! Nesvitski, you blockhead!" came a hoarse voice from behind.

Nesvitski turned and saw, about fifteen paces back but cut off by the solid, moving mass of infantry, Vaska Denisov—red-faced and shaggy, his cap shoved to the back of his black head, a cloak thrown dashingly over one shoulder.

"Tell these devils—these fiends—to let me through!" Denisov shouted, clearly in a fury, his coal-black eyes with their bloodshot whites glittering and rolling as he waved his sheathed saber in a small, bare hand as red as his face.
"Vaska!" Nesvitski called back joyfully. "What's going on?"

"The squadwon can't get thwough!" Vaska Denisov shouted, baring his white teeth fiercely and spurring his black thoroughbred Arab, which flicked its ears as bayonets grazed it and snorted, spraying white foam from its bit, stamping the bridge planks with its hooves—looking ready to vault right over the railings if its rider allowed it. "What is this? They're like sheep! Just like sheep! Out of the way! Let us through! You there with the cart—I'll cut you down with my saber!" he yelled, actually drawing his saber and brandishing it.
The soldiers crushed against each other with terrified faces, and Denisov managed to reach Nesvitski.
"How is it you're not drunk today?" Nesvitski asked when Denisov had ridden up alongside.
"They don't even give you time to dwink!" Denisov answered. "They keep dwagging the wegiment back and forth all day. If we're going to fight, then let's fight. But God only knows what this is."
"What a dandy you look today!" said Nesvitski, eyeing Denisov's new cloak and saddle cloth.
Denisov grinned, pulled a handkerchief from his sabretache that gave off a waft of perfume, and pressed it to Nesvitski's nose.
"Of course! I'm going into action! I've shaved, bwushed my teeth, and put on cologne."

The imposing bulk of Nesvitski, trailed by his Cossack, combined with Denisov's fierce determination as he swung his sword and shouted like a madman, had such an effect that they managed to force their way through to the far side of the bridge and halt the infantry. At the bridgehead, Nesvitski found the colonel he needed to deliver the order to, and having done so, rode back.

Having cleared the way, Denisov stopped at the end of the bridge. Casually reining in his stallion—which was neighing and pawing the ground, eager to rejoin the other horses—he watched his squadron approaching. The clang of hooves, as if several horses were galloping at once, rang out on the bridge planks, and the squadron, officers in front and men four abreast, spread across the bridge and began emerging on his side.

The infantry soldiers who had been held up stood in the trampled mud near the bridge and watched with that particular mixture of hostility, detachment, and mockery that troops of different branches typically feel when they encounter one another—watching the clean, smart hussars ride past in neat formation.
"Pretty boys! Only good for a parade!" one said.
"What use are they? Just marched around for show!" another remarked.
"Don't kick up the dust, you foot-sloggers!" joked a hussar whose prancing horse had splattered mud on several infantrymen.

"I'd like to see you after a two-day march with a knapsack! Those fancy trousers would get worn through soon enough," said an infantryman, wiping mud off his face with his sleeve. "Sitting up there, you look more like a bird than a man."
"Hey, Zikin, they ought to put you on a horse. You'd be a sight!" said a corporal, teasing a scrawny little soldier bowed under the weight of his knapsack.
"Stick a branch between your legs—that'll do for your horse!" the hussar shouted back.
